## Methods

Datasets

fMRI data. BOLD signals are obtained from an open dataset DIR45, which are collected using a Siemens
MAGNETOM Verio scanner 3.0-Tesla from three healthy subjects. In image presentation experiments,
each subject viewed 1,250 unique images of natural scenes. These image stimuli are drawn from 200
representative object categories of the ImageNet dataset36, with 150 categories used for training and 50
for testing. Each training image stimulus (8 images per category, totaling 1,200 images) is repeated 5
times, and each test image stimulus (1 image per category) is repeated 24 times, leading to 6,000 and
1,200 image-fMRI instances, respectively. More fMRI data preprocessing details can be found in the
original paper. In this study, we focused on voxels from brain visual areas including the lateral occipital
complex (LOC), fusiform face area (FFA), and parahippocampal place area (PPA), which are known to
be part of the higher visual cortex (HVC)24.

Natural images. The natural images used in this study were drawn from three datasets: ImageNet-21K36,
the THINGS object concept and image dataset46, and the Common Objects in Context (COCO) dataset38.
1) Corresponding to the BOLD signals of the DIR45, we collected natural images including 200 object
categories from Image-21K for mental representation-guided supervision of models, where 150 categories,
comprising 206,848 object images, were used as the training set, while the remaining 50 categories,
totaling 66,067 object images (275–2115 images per category), constitute the test set. Note that the object
categories are the same as those in the DIR, and there is no overlap between the training and test sets. 2)
The images of 1,854 diverse object concepts, collected from the THINGS dataset, were leveraged to
perform triplet odd-one-out tasks. 3) The COCO dataset, a large-scale image dataset including detailed
annotations of the images such as image captions, was used to train the text decoder in our manifold
analysis experiments.

Overall, we leveraged four public datasets to evaluate the effectiveness of our approach. The visual stimuli
used in the fMRI dataset (DIR) are drawn from ImageNet and are therefore independent of the THINGS
and COCO datasets. This ensures that the test samples in triplet odd-one-out tasks (Fig. 4e) and semantic
reconstruction (Fig. 6) are out-of-distribution (OOD). For mental representation-guided supervised
models, we only employed 150 categories in the DIR dataset for training. The THINGS dataset provides
4.7 million human triplet odd-one-out responses across 1,854 object concepts. This greatly surpasses the
200 object categories in the DIR dataset, making it highly suitable for testing whether mental
representation-guided supervision enhances the alignment between models and humans (Fig. 4f). Unlike
ImageNet, which only provides simple category labels, the COCO dataset includes detailed image
description, enabling the training of a text decoder to reconstruct semantic information from mental
representation-guided supervised models.

Statistical analysis

In this study, we applied the two-tailed paired t-test and repeated random sub-sampling validation (also

accomplished using seaborn, a Python data visualization library, and statannotations, which is used to add
statistical significance annotations on seaborn plots. The detailed P values for all comparisons are

Noteworthy results: (reviewers' summary)
Recent advances in deep neural networks (DNNs), especially large models (LMs) have skyrocketed their image and text
understanding as well as generation and classification performance. However, imitating the in depth interpretation and
abstract reasoning capacities of humans remains a major challenge.
This study challenges the ability of large neural network model architectures to capture and learn generalised concepts.
Since DNNs are usually trained to perform well on a clearly defined task, such as classification, they tend to lack the human-
like abstraction capacity. To this end, a brain-in-the-loop supervision framework was introduced, which aligns the DNN
embeddings with human brain activation structure. Specifically, fMRI brain signals were compared to the DNN image
embeddings via an encoder and graph neural network architecture. The improvement of generalization capabilities was
demonstrated in a series of tailored experiments providing evidence and supporting the claim that the semantic coherence of
DNNs can be enhanced by incorporating human conceptual structure into their training. Improved performance also involved
one-shot learning and out-of-distribution recognition.
Validity and Significance
This paper introduces a novel method of leveraging human brain-based representations to improve AI systems toward
human-level understanding. An iterative graph matching routine is introduced utilising Wasserstein distance and Gromov-
Wasserstein (GW) distance based loss functions (line 630 and 642 in the main text). The validity of the results is tested on
several state-of-the-art models including CLIP, SimCLR and DINOv2 showing that one-shot classification accuracy
improves significantly when brain-in-the-loop supervision is deployed, particularly for abstract concepts (see Fig.1 a-c). The
statistical robustness of the results is confirmed by two-tailed paired t-tests with adequate P-value scores.
Notably, the framework paves the way for integrating human-like abstraction capabilities into AI by means of its structural
alignment with biological neural activity.
Overall, the paper is very well written, with a lot of numerical results, providing a consistent picture about what has been
gained by including sparse brain-in-the-loop information into AI models.
Methodology and Data
In order to test the concept understanding of DNNs (without brain-in-the-loop) a one-shot learning experiment (Fig.1, a-c)
was conducted for concrete and abstract concepts and three different architectures with varying sizes. Increasing the model
parameter number yielded an improvement in the concrete concept classification, but only a negligible advantage in abstract
concept classification.
For the remaining set of experiments the networks were integrated into a composite architecture together with the fMRI
encoder of brain signals, training the encoders across 150 training categories and evaluating with 50 unseen ones. The
Silhouette Coefficients were computed to measure representation quality for concrete vs. abstract concepts demonstrating
enhanced conceptual alignment with brain-in-the-loop (Fig.3).
Furthermore, conceptual similarity matrices (CSM) of DNN’s representations with brain-in-the-loop demonstrate higher
similarity to WordNet’s conceptual hierarchy and odd-one-out accuracy rises by ~6% compared to the base model (Fig.4).
One shot classification and out-of-distribution recognition with brain-in-the-loop display higher accuracy for all considered
DNNs (Fig.5) and consistency tests on a PCA manifold also corroborate improved semantic robustness with brain-in-the-
loop supervision (Fig.6). Moreover, multiple tests, such as semantic summarisation, focusing on the conceptual manifold
confirmed its cognitive-level consistency and ordered organization of concepts. (also Fig. 6).
Altogether, the initial assumption that incorporating brain-in-the-loop optimization into large DNN image classifiers promotes
the model’s abstract conceptual understanding is more than well supported by the experimental evidence.

Along with the paper, both the code and data are provided which should enable good reproducibility of the results.

object images but only 6,000 fMRI signals were used (see Methods line 492 and 501 and Supplementary Text). Even

Minor details

This work sets out to investigate whether Brain-in-the-Loop supervision can elevate the performance of cognitive
generalization for Large Language Models.
It proposes to enhance the cognitive ability of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) by using the structural organization of the
human brain as a supervisor. Initial findings showed that increasing the parameter size of DNNs improved their
understanding of concrete concepts but there was little effect on abstract concept understanding.
Increasing parameter sizes enhances DNN's understanding of concrete but not abstract concepts was observed in DNN

• Enhancement of abstract concept understanding with brain-in-the-loop

These results are all clearly described although the reader is often referred to information in the supplementary information.

This is a very good piece of research that is well motivated and quite clearly communicated. The statistical results are well

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications.

You previously reviewed this paper and raised several concerns. The authors have now submitted a revised manuscript along with a detailed point-by-point response. Your task is to write your updated review after carefully reading:
  1. The revised paper
  2. Your original Round 1 review
  3. The authors' point-by-point response

In your updated review, explicitly state which concerns have been adequately addressed and which remain outstanding. Be specific.

## Paper

## Abstract

Recent advancements in deep neural networks (DNNs), particularly large-scale language models, have
demonstrated remarkable capabilities in image and natural language understanding. Although scaling up
model parameters with increasing volume of training data has progressively improved DNN capabilities,
achieving complex cognitive abilities—such as understanding abstract concepts, reasoning, and adapting
to novel scenarios, which are intrinsic to human cognition—remains a major challenge. In this study, we
show that mental representation-guided supervised learning, utilizing a small set of brain signals, can
effectively transfer human conceptual structures to DNNs, significantly enhancing their comprehension
of abstract and even unseen concepts. Experimental results further indicate that the enhanced cognitive
capabilities lead to substantial performance gains in challenging tasks, including few-shot/zero-shot
learning and out-of-distribution recognition, while also yielding highly interpretable concept
representations. These findings highlight that mental representation-guided supervision can effectively
augment the complex cognitive abilities of large models, offering a promising pathway toward developing
more human-like cognitive abilities in artificial systems.

---

## Introduction

Humans live in a world full of ever-changing objects, which requires us to constantly learn new concepts
from a variety of sensory information and systematically structure our experiential knowledge of the
physical world1,2. This ability helps us organize our knowledge and make sense of the world, allowing us
to recognize new things and adapt to new situations. For years, artificial intelligence (AI) researchers have
tried to build systems that understand the world like humans do3–7. Although Fodor and Pylyshyn8
suggested that neural networks are not plausible cognitive models because they lack the systematicity of
mental representations, deep neural networks (DNNs), especially with the help of large-scale datasets and
large models (LMs)9–11, did achieved higher systematic level ability. The question of whether and how
neural networks could achieve human-like cognitive ability has sparked a vigorous debate spanning
several decades1.

Current DNNs or LMs still struggle to match human-like cognition12. Scaling up data and model size has
primarily improved performance in well-defined tasks like classification, object detection, and content
generation13–15. However, when it comes to human-like cognitive abilities—particularly the understanding
and generalization of novel concepts—current models still fall short1,12,16. Moreover, increasing model
size does not consistently enhance these capabilities, and in some cases, performance even plateaus or
degrades12,17, highlighting a fundamental limitation in achieving high-level cognition18. Recalling Fodor
and Pylyshyn's opinion8, the systematicity of mental representations might be an important but overlooked
component for neural networks to obtain human-like cognition.

Here, we proposed to enhance the cognitive ability of DNNs by leveraging the structural organization of
the human brain as a supervisory signal. Our initial observations revealed that while increasing the
parameter size of DNNs improved their understanding of concrete concepts (Fig. 1a), it had little effect
on abstract concepts (Fig. 1b, c). This limitation stems from DNNs' inability to capture the internal
relationships among concepts and their lack of abstraction and conceptualization capabilities (Fig. 1d, e).
Motivated by this insight, we developed a mental representation-guided supervision framework to directly
transfer the brain's cognitive structure to DNNs. Remarkably, we found that aligning the structural
representations of DNNs with the brain using only a small set of objects significantly enhanced their
ability to understand abstract concepts (Fig. 1b, c), with the learned cognitive structures generalizing well
to unseen concepts. This process led to the emergence of human-like conceptual hierarchies in DNNs,
closely resembling WordNet19—even without explicit constraints to match it. The proposed framework
consistently improved performance across a range of challenging tasks, including few-shot/zero-shot
learning20,21 and out-of-distribution recognition22, while also producing highly interpretable concept
representations. These results were robust across diverse DNN architectures, including SimCLR23, CLIP10,
and DINOv29. Our findings suggest a promising new direction for developing AI systems that think more
like humans, moving beyond the limitations of current approaches that rely solely on scaling data and
model complexity.

---

## Results

Increasing the parameter size of DNNs enhances their understanding of concrete but not abstract
concepts

To assess the concept understanding capabilities of DNNs, we first conducted one-shot learning tasks for
both concrete and abstract concepts. The concrete concepts comprised 50 classes, including objects such
as sock and swan, while the abstract concepts consisted of 8 higher-level categories, such
as clothing and bird (Supplementary Fig. S1). We employed the one-shot learning task, where for each
class, one image was randomly selected for training, and the remaining images were used for testing (see
Supplementary for details). The abstract concept task posed a significantly greater challenge, as it required
models to generalize to unseen objects within a broader category. For instance, the model had to infer that
an owl belongs to the class bird when provided with a swan as the only example.

We evaluated several DNN architectures, including SimCLR23, DINOv29, and CLIP10, across varying
parameter scales (see Supplementary for details). For concrete concepts, we observed a consistent
improvement in one-shot classification performance as the number of parameters increased (Fig. 1a). In
contrast, for abstract concepts, increasing model parameters yielded only marginal improvements or even
led to performance degradation (Fig. 1b, c). For instance, with the DINOv2 model, performance on
concrete concepts significantly improved from 74.94% to 85.87% (P = 1.78 × 10−76, two-tailed paired t-
test) as trainable parameters increased from 22.06 million to 304.37 million. However, for abstract
concepts, the performance gain from scaling parameters was negligible or even negative, with
performance dropping significantly from 54.37% to 52.82% as parameters increased from 22.06 million
to 304.37 million (P = 6.66 × 10−4, two-tailed paired t-test). Similar trends were observed across SimCLR,
and CLIP models. These results revealed that while increasing the parameter size of DNNs improved their
performance on concrete concepts, it did not substantially enhance their ability to understand abstract
concepts.

To investigate the underlying reasons for the performance disparity between concrete and abstract
concepts, we analyzed the representational dissimilarity matrices (RDMs; see Supplementary for
computational details) to visualize the conceptual relationships (representational distances) learned by
each model. We first examined the brain's RDM, derived from fMRI voxels from higher visual cortex
(HVC) areas24 including the lateral occipital complex (LOC), fusiform face area (FFA), and
parahippocampal place area (PPA), as a reference for a well-structured conceptual framework (Fig. 1d,
see Supplementary Fig. S2a, b for RIDMs derived from other brain regions).

We observed that the brain's RDM using voxels from HVC revealed two distinct clusters (Fig. 1d)
corresponding to living beings (red square) and non-living objects (purple square), reflecting a robust
semantic understanding of the concepts. When comparing the RDMs of DNNs (using the final output
representations), only the CLIP model exhibited partial alignment with the brain's RDM, showing a
discernible cluster for living beings (Fig. 1e). In contrast, the other models, while demonstrating strong
discrimination of concrete concepts (evidenced by superior classification capabilities), failed to capture
the broader semantic clusters of living and non-living entities. This suggests that without a meaningful
understanding of the relationships between concrete concepts, DNNs struggle to generalize to abstract
concepts, highlighting a critical limitation in their cognitive capabilities. We also found that using fMRI
signals from HVC to guide the model yielded significantly higher classification performance compared
to using voxels from the lower visual cortex (LVC) or the entire visual cortex (Supplementary Fig. S2c).
These results provide further evidence that the semantic structures in higher-level visual areas are critical
for model optimization.

Mental representation-guided supervision enables DNNs to learn human-like conceptual
representations

Previous analysis indicated that the inability to capture internal relationships between concepts might be
a key factor limiting DNNs' understanding of abstract concepts—a capability inherently embedded in
human cognition2. Instead of further scaling up model parameters, we proposed a mental representation-
guided supervision framework to transfer human conceptual structures to DNNs.

We hypothesized that the conceptual structure of objects could be represented with a graph, and both the
pretrained LMs and the human brain have formed their own conceptual structures based on learning. Then,
given a set of objects, we can align the LMs' conceptual graph to the human brain's with a graph
matching25 approach. Here we built an iterative optimization framework (Fig. 2a) to reshape the
conceptual structure of LMs through two main steps that are performed in an alternative manner: 1)
seeking the optimal correspondences between LMs and the human brain representations; 2) updating
representations to maximize structural similarity (Fig. 2b). To this end, our architecture consists of three
learnable modules, i.e., a fMRI encoder, an image encoder, and a graph neural network26. By differentiable
design, gradients can be backpropagated from the matching layers to the encoders during the training
procedure (see Methods for details).

While the number of concepts is large in the real world, we found that by aligning the conceptual graph
with a small set of objects, the alignment was well generated to unseen concepts. Here, using the CLIP
model as an example, we performed alignment between the brain and the CLIP model across 150 concrete
object categories, and evaluated the distances between the representations of the brain and DNN with 50
unseen classes (see Methods). As shown in Fig. 2c, as the mental representation-guided supervision
process evolves, the distance between brain and DNN representations decreased consistently for both the
concepts in the training concepts and unseen concepts in mostly linear processes (R2 = 0.86, Pearson's r
= –0.93 for training, and R2 = 0.83, Pearson's r = –0.91 for unseen), revealing good generalization to
unseen objects. The RDM of the 50 unseen classes also demonstrated similarity to brain's RDM
(Supplementary Fig. S3a), with a better conceptual structure of objects (Supplementary Fig. S3b, c). These
results suggested that mental representation-guided supervision learning approach effectively transferred
human's conceptual structures to DNNs.

Enhancement of abstract concept understanding

We next evaluated the model's ability to understand abstract concepts with and without mental
representation-guided supervision. As illustrated in Fig. 1a and b (Bottom), models trained with mental
representation-guided supervision demonstrated significant improvements in one-shot learning tasks for
abstract concepts (P < 0.0001, two-tailed paired t-test, n = 100 independent runs).

To further assess the understanding of abstract concepts at different levels of abstraction, we employed
the Silhouette Coefficient (SC)27 to measure the quality of representations on 50 unseen classes (n =
66,067 test samples). The SC score, ranging from −1 to 1, evaluates how well each sample fits within its
own cluster (intra-cluster distance) and how well it is separated from other clusters (nearest-cluster
distance). A higher SC indicates that objects within the same concept have similar representations, while
objects from different concepts are well-separated, reflecting a better understanding of conceptual
relationships. As shown in Fig. 3a, without mental representation-guided supervision, models exhibited
strong representation ability for concrete concepts (SC = 0.231 for the 50 leaf nodes) but showed a marked
decline in performance for middle-level (SC = 0.144 for the 8 middle-level nodes) and high-level concepts
(SC = 0.044 for the 3 high-level nodes). This suggests that while models excel at understanding concrete
concepts, they struggle with abstract ones.

In contrast, with mental representation-guided supervision, concept representation improved significantly
across all three abstraction levels (Fig. 3a, P < 0.0001, two-tailed paired t-test), particularly for abstract
concepts. The SC increased from 0.144 to 0.239 for middle-level concepts and from 0.044 to 0.127 for
high-level concepts. Notably, we observed a nearly linear correlation between the degree of structural
alignment (measured by Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) distance28, which quantifies the dissimilarity
between two metric spaces by comparing the pairwise relational structures; see Methods for
computational details) and the SC score (Fig. 3b). This strongly suggests that the enhanced conceptual
understanding stems from the alignment of the model's representational structure with the brain's
conceptual framework. Further improvements could be achieved by pushing the models' representational
structures to be more consistent with the brain. Together, these findings demonstrate that mental
representation-guided supervision effectively enhances models' capacity to conceptualize abstract
categories.

Emergence of human-like conceptual hierarchy

We further assessed the similarity between the conceptual hierarchy structures of humans and models
using the 50 unseen concepts. To this end, we utilized WordNet19, a comprehensive lexical database that
encodes conceptual-semantic relationships, as a representation of human conceptual hierarchy (Fig. 4a).
We compared this structure of the models with the 50 unseen concepts. Our analysis revealed that models
trained with mental representation-guided supervision exhibited concept similarity matrices (CSMs)
highly aligned with WordNet, whereas models without such supervision showed no such alignment (Fig.
4b; see Supplementary Tab. S1 for the row/column labels of CSMs). Note that each entry of the CSM
quantifies the similarity between a pair of concepts (see Supplementary for computational details). These
findings were consistent across different DNN architectures and brain signals from multiple subjects (Fig.
4b-d and Supplementary Fig. S4).

Additionally, we found that mental representation-guided supervision enabled models to exhibit human-
like judgments in concept similarity tasks. Specifically, we employed a triplet odd-one-out task, where
participants (human or DNN model) were presented with three images and asked to select the least related
one (Fig. 4e). Human judgment data were sourced from the THINGS database29, which contains 4.7
million triplet odd-one-out judgments across 1,854 objects from 12,340 participants. We compared the
similarity between human and model responses (see Supplementary for details). Results showed that
mental representation-guided supervision significantly improved the alignment between human
judgments and model behaviors (Fig. 4f), with accuracy increasing from 43.74% to 49.94% (P = 7.56 ×
10−97, two-tailed paired t-test).

Many current DNN models can be easily deceived by targeted pixel-level perturbations (adversarial
attacks), whereas humans are remarkably robust against such perturbations. The lack of robustness
highlights that DNNs fall short of human-like understanding concepts. Therefore, we used projected
gradient descent (PGD) attacks30 to evaluate the robustness of mental representation-guided supervised
models (Fig. 4g, see Supplementary for details). We observed that human-like conceptual hierarchy leads
to increased adversarial robustness for CLIP-base on abstract concepts, with adversarial accuracy
increasing from 50.82% to 68.95% (3 abstract concepts; P = 4.01 × 10−71, two-tailed paired t-test) and
10.98% to 14.79% (8 abstract concepts; P = 5.94 × 10−18, two-tailed paired t-test). Together, these results
demonstrate that mental representation-guided supervision enables models to develop human-like
conceptual hierarchy structures, significantly enhancing their ability to conceptualize abstract categories.

Human-like conceptual hierarchy enhances performance in complex cognitive tasks

We demonstrated that models endowed with human-like conceptual hierarchy structures achieve
significant performance improvements across a variety of complex cognitive tasks.

One-shot learning (OSL). We first evaluated the one-shot learning capabilities of the models at different
abstraction levels. As was mentioned, a central challenge in one-shot classification, is to rapidly
understand the concepts from only one example31. The problem can be more difficult when the concepts
become more abstract (Fig. 5a, see Supplementary). When there are only two abstract concepts of living
thing and non-living thing, CLIP-base with mental representation-guided supervision achieved an average
improvement of 20.5 ± 1.3% (mean ± s.d., averaged across S1-S3, P < 0.0001 for all subjects, two-tailed
paired t-test) in OSL performance, outperforming baseline models with 4.9 times more parameters (Fig.
5b). Mental representation-guided supervision achieved consistent performance gains across different
DNN architectures (CLIP10, SimCLR23 and DINOv29) and supervision using brain signals from different
subjects (Fig. 5b and Supplementary Fig. S5). Moreover, we found a nearly linear correlation between the
degree of structural alignment (measured by GW distance28) and the one-shot classification accuracy,
consistent across supervision using brain signals from different subjects (Supplementary Fig. S6).

Generalized out-of-distribution (OOD) recognition. Next, we examined how mental representation-
guided supervision enhanced the robustness of generalized OOD recognition (Fig. 5c, see Supplementary).
We defined a series of OOD recognition tasks (31 tasks, see Supplementary Tab. S2), which assess the
conceptual extrapolation ability of DNNs from minimal category supervision, such as determining
whether unseen categories (e.g., "bowling" and "carriage") should be classified as a broader category (e.g.,
"non-animal"). These tasks require models to capture high-level semantic structures that align with the
hierarchical structure of human conceptual knowledge. As shown in Fig. 5d, mental representation-guided
supervision significantly improved OOD robustness, yielding performance increases of 11.5 ± 4.7%, 13.6
± 9.3%, 9.1 ± 8.3% (mean ± s.d., averaged across 3 subjects and 31 tasks, P < 0.0001 for all subjects,
two-tailed paired t-test) for CLIP-base, SimCLR-base and DINOv2-base, respectively, without the need
for extensive supervision labels. Similar improvement trends can be found in different architectures across
varying parameter scales and supervision using brain signals from different subjects (Fig. 5d).

Brain-to-image and image-to-image retrieval. To intuitively assess the quality of the learned
representations, we evaluated the effectiveness of mental representation-guided supervision for both
brain-to-image (Fig. 5e, see Supplementary) and image-to-image (Fig. 5g, see Supplementary) retrieval
tasks. Brain-to-image retrieval, a common benchmark for neural decoding models24,32,33, evaluates the
ability to reconstruct perceived stimuli (n = 50 visual stimuli) from brain signals. Our approach
consistently improved decoding performance, achieving an average increase of 7.34%–26.67% in 50-way
retrieval across all subjects compared to existing decoding methods33–35 (Fig. 5f). Qualitative analysis of
brain-to-image retrieval on a subset of ImageNet-21K36 (n = 66,067 test samples, Supplementary Fig.
S7a-c) indicated the concept representations of DNNs can be predicted from fMRI patterns derived using
our mental representation-guided supervision framework. For example, the fMRI pattern evoked from an
image of "a man lying on a hammock" can be the image of "a child lying on the baby carriage" (the 5th
row, Supplementary Fig. S7a). In the case of "harp" (the 6th row, Supplementary Fig. S7a), although the
top retrievals fall into the wrong concrete categories, they are all related to "musical instruments". Similar
results can be found in most instances across different subjects (Supplementary Fig. S7b, c).

In image-to-image retrieval tasks (Fig. 5g, h), mental representation-guided supervision enabled models
to retrieve semantically similar objects despite significant visual differences, even when these objects
belonged to different predefined categories. For example, an image of a "beer mug" successfully retrieved
images sharing attributes like "cup" or "jug" from distinct categories (Fig. 5h, top row). Similar results
were observed across most instances, highlighting the model's enhanced ability to capture semantic
relationships beyond superficial visual features. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that human-like
conceptual hierarchy structures, facilitated by mental representation-guided supervision, significantly
enhance model performance in complex cognitive tasks.

Cognitive-level consistency of the learned conceptual manifold

To evaluate whether the latent embedding spaces, shaped by mental representation-guided supervision,
capture typical judgements for concepts, we generated a low-dimensional PCA-based space (conceptual
manifold; see Supplementary for details), and trained a GPT-2-based37 text decoder on the COCO
dataset38 (see Supplementary for details). This conceptual manifold allows us to assess cognitive-level
consistency for both seen and unseen points in the latent space, while the decoder reconstructs the
semantics of a given representation point as a sequence of words, enabling a detailed analysis of the
manifold's properties.

Local semantic consistency. We first assessed the local semantic consistency of the manifold, which
measures whether similar concepts are clustered together in the representation space. To this end, we
designed an out-of-distribution semantic coherence test (see Supplementary for details), evaluating the
semantic consistency and similarity between newly generated samples and their nearest real neighbors in
PCA space (Fig. 6a). This task can also be considered a zero-shot test of semantic coherence, since the
evaluations are performed in novel categories without explicit training. Note that in this study, zero-shot
(learning) means that performing a task on unseen samples, where the model is trained only on known
samples—not learning without any data. As shown in Fig. 6b, we found that the 2-D PCA points sampled
from different conceptual regions show strong semantic correlations with the real samples. For example,
we can reconstruct the semantics of T-shirt and tie within the "clothing" region and generate the semantics
of truck near the region associated with "vehicles". In contrast, models without brain supervision produced
semantically meaningless reconstructions (Supplementary Fig. S8a). By using 8 abstract categories as
ground-truth, we found that mental representation-guided supervision significantly enhanced local
semantic coherence, with semantic consistency accuracy improving by 15.9% and semantic similarity
scores increasing by 6.2% on average compared to the model without supervision (P < 0.0001, two-tailed
paired t-test, Fig. 6c).

Intersections between different concepts. We further investigated whether intersections between
different concepts yield meaningful reconstructions. By generating new points through interpolation
between two real samples from distinct concepts (Fig. 6d), we observed that the reconstructed semantics
aligned well with human intuition, exhibiting smooth and realistic transitions (Fig. 6e). For instance,
transitioning between "iPod" and "video recorder" resulted in a logical semantic shift from "television" to
"video recorder" (Fig. 6e, left), while interpolating between vehicles and ungulate animals produced the
concept of "horse" (Fig. 6e, right). Qualitative analysis indicates most of the key features of these concepts
can be effectively captured with a limited number of principal components, which is also reflected in the
reconstruction error and explained variance ratio (Supplementary Fig. S8b). These findings suggest that
mental representation-guided supervision ensures the conceptual manifold is semantically continuous and
smooth, enhancing the model's cognitive generalization capabilities.

Concept summarization and arithmetic. Finally, we evaluated the original latent space using two highly
challenging tasks: concept summarization (Fig. 6f) and concept arithmetic (Fig. 6h), which involves linear
operations on latent embeddings (see Supplementary for details). For concept summarization, the model
was tasked with generating a sentence to describe multiple input images. As shown in Fig. 6g, the
regulated manifold enabled the model to infer shared behavioral details and the number of objects. For
example, given a set of images depicting different types of animals lying on grass, the decoder with mental
representation-guided supervision was able to reconstruct the sentence of "animal laying on a grassy area".
Given a set of images, each depicting a close-up of a pair of different animals standing on grass, the
decoder successfully reconstructed the text "two animals standing in a grassy area".

For concept arithmetic (Fig. 6h), we tested whether mental representation-guided supervision could steer
generated captions toward desired conceptual directions through subtraction and addition operations. For
example, subtracting "motorcycle" and adding "horse" shifted the semantics from "a man riding a
motorcycle" to "a man riding a horse" (Fig. 6i, first case). Similarly, removing "dog" from "a dog playing
with a frisbee" and adding "a young girl" yielded "a young girl is playing with a frisbee" (Fig. 6i, second
case). In the third case, subtracting "banana" and adding "cell phone" transformed "a young girl holding
a banana" into "a young girl holding a cell phone."

These results demonstrate that mental representation-guided supervision produces a low-dimensional
conceptual manifold that aligns with human judgments, enabling accurate and intuitive descriptions of
objects along semantically meaningful dimensions. This advancement highlights the potential of brain-
guided approaches in creating models with enhanced cognitive generalization and interpretability.

---

## Methods

Datasets

fMRI data. BOLD signals are obtained from an open dataset DIR45, which are collected using a Siemens
MAGNETOM Verio scanner 3.0-Tesla from three healthy subjects. In image presentation experiments,
each subject viewed 1,250 unique images of natural scenes. These image stimuli are drawn from 200
representative object categories of the ImageNet dataset36, with 150 categories used for training and 50
for testing. Each training image stimulus (8 images per category, totaling 1,200 images) is repeated 5

Model architecture. Technically, like most representation learning practices, our first component
employs two nonlinear encoders (here, a ViT50 and a multilayer perceptron but can take any other form)
to map brain signals (fMRI) and image embeddings to new latent spaces (Fig. 2a). Next, a GNN34,51,52
with multi-head attention, which learns node representation for both fMRI and images (parameters are
shared across modalities; see Supplementary for details) is leveraged to predict an assignment matrix with
minimal Wasserstein distance47, resulting in initial correspondences between brain and model
representations. The representations in latent spaces are considered as graph nodes (entities). To reshape
embedding spaces of DNNs, we leverage a differentiable sampler (based on re-parametrization technique
Gumbel Softmax49) with the similarity scores between entities to construct local structures for each
putative correspondence. It is worth noting that the procedure of structure (edge) construction is
"dynamic" since node representations are evolving through the update of neural network parameters
during training. See Supplementary for the architecture configuration and hyperparameter settings.

By using relaxation techniques48,49, all calculation and optimization processes in the pipeline are
differentiable, enabling gradients to be backpropagated from the matching layers to the encoders. We
conduct mental representation-guided supervision on the DIR dataset. The stimuli (150 training categories
and 50 test categories) in DIR dataset are identical to those used in the GOD dataset24 but contain a larger
number of evoked fMRI recordings (6,000 training samples and 1,200 test samples). See Supplementary

This paper introduces a novel method of leveraging human brain-based representations to improve AI systems toward

## Paper

## Abstract

Recent advancements in deep neural networks (DNNs), particularly large-scale language models, have
demonstrated remarkable capabilities in image and natural language understanding. Although scaling up
model parameters with increasing volume of training data has progressively improved DNN capabilities,
achieving complex cognitive abilities—such as understanding abstract concepts, reasoning, and adapting
to novel scenarios, which are intrinsic to human cognition—remains a major challenge. In this study, we
show that mental representation-guided supervised learning, utilizing a small set of brain signals, can
effectively transfer human conceptual structures to DNNs, significantly enhancing their comprehension
of abstract and even unseen concepts. Experimental results further indicate that the enhanced cognitive
capabilities lead to substantial performance gains in challenging tasks, including few-shot/zero-shot
learning and out-of-distribution recognition, while also yielding highly interpretable concept
representations. These findings highlight that mental representation-guided supervision can effectively
augment the complex cognitive abilities of large models, offering a promising pathway toward developing
more human-like cognitive abilities in artificial systems.

---

## Introduction

Humans live in a world full of ever-changing objects, which requires us to constantly learn new concepts
from a variety of sensory information and systematically structure our experiential knowledge of the
physical world1,2. This ability helps us organize our knowledge and make sense of the world, allowing us
to recognize new things and adapt to new situations. For years, artificial intelligence (AI) researchers have
tried to build systems that understand the world like humans do3–7. Although Fodor and Pylyshyn8
suggested that neural networks are not plausible cognitive models because they lack the systematicity of
mental representations, deep neural networks (DNNs), especially with the help of large-scale datasets and
large models (LMs)9–11, did achieved higher systematic level ability. The question of whether and how
neural networks could achieve human-like cognitive ability has sparked a vigorous debate spanning
several decades1.

Current DNNs or LMs still struggle to match human-like cognition12. Scaling up data and model size has
primarily improved performance in well-defined tasks like classification, object detection, and content
generation13–15. However, when it comes to human-like cognitive abilities—particularly the understanding
and generalization of novel concepts—current models still fall short1,12,16. Moreover, increasing model
size does not consistently enhance these capabilities, and in some cases, performance even plateaus or
degrades12,17, highlighting a fundamental limitation in achieving high-level cognition18. Recalling Fodor
and Pylyshyn's opinion8, the systematicity of mental representations might be an important but overlooked
component for neural networks to obtain human-like cognition.

Here, we proposed to enhance the cognitive ability of DNNs by leveraging the structural organization of
the human brain as a supervisory signal. Our initial observations revealed that while increasing the
parameter size of DNNs improved their understanding of concrete concepts (Fig. 1a), it had little effect
on abstract concepts (Fig. 1b, c). This limitation stems from DNNs' inability to capture the internal
relationships among concepts and their lack of abstraction and conceptualization capabilities (Fig. 1d, e).
Motivated by this insight, we developed a mental representation-guided supervision framework to directly
transfer the brain's cognitive structure to DNNs. Remarkably, we found that aligning the structural
representations of DNNs with the brain using only a small set of objects significantly enhanced their
ability to understand abstract concepts (Fig. 1b, c), with the learned cognitive structures generalizing well
to unseen concepts. This process led to the emergence of human-like conceptual hierarchies in DNNs,
closely resembling WordNet19—even without explicit constraints to match it. The proposed framework
consistently improved performance across a range of challenging tasks, including few-shot/zero-shot
learning20,21 and out-of-distribution recognition22, while also producing highly interpretable concept
representations. These results were robust across diverse DNN architectures, including SimCLR23, CLIP10,
and DINOv29. Our findings suggest a promising new direction for developing AI systems that think more
like humans, moving beyond the limitations of current approaches that rely solely on scaling data and
model complexity.

---

## Results

Increasing the parameter size of DNNs enhances their understanding of concrete but not abstract
concepts

To assess the concept understanding capabilities of DNNs, we first conducted one-shot learning tasks for
both concrete and abstract concepts. The concrete concepts comprised 50 classes, including objects such
as sock and swan, while the abstract concepts consisted of 8 higher-level categories, such
as clothing and bird (Supplementary Fig. S1). We employed the one-shot learning task, where for each
class, one image was randomly selected for training, and the remaining images were used for testing (see
Supplementary for details). The abstract concept task posed a significantly greater challenge, as it required
models to generalize to unseen objects within a broader category. For instance, the model had to infer that
an owl belongs to the class bird when provided with a swan as the only example.

We evaluated several DNN architectures, including SimCLR23, DINOv29, and CLIP10, across varying
parameter scales (see Supplementary for details). For concrete concepts, we observed a consistent
improvement in one-shot classification performance as the number of parameters increased (Fig. 1a). In
contrast, for abstract concepts, increasing model parameters yielded only marginal improvements or even
led to performance degradation (Fig. 1b, c). For instance, with the DINOv2 model, performance on
concrete concepts significantly improved from 74.94% to 85.87% (P = 1.78 × 10−76, two-tailed paired t-
test) as trainable parameters increased from 22.06 million to 304.37 million. However, for abstract
concepts, the performance gain from scaling parameters was negligible or even negative, with
performance dropping significantly from 54.37% to 52.82% as parameters increased from 22.06 million
to 304.37 million (P = 6.66 × 10−4, two-tailed paired t-test). Similar trends were observed across SimCLR,
and CLIP models. These results revealed that while increasing the parameter size of DNNs improved their
performance on concrete concepts, it did not substantially enhance their ability to understand abstract
concepts.

To investigate the underlying reasons for the performance disparity between concrete and abstract
concepts, we analyzed the representational dissimilarity matrices (RDMs; see Supplementary for
computational details) to visualize the conceptual relationships (representational distances) learned by
each model. We first examined the brain's RDM, derived from fMRI voxels from higher visual cortex
(HVC) areas24 including the lateral occipital complex (LOC), fusiform face area (FFA), and
parahippocampal place area (PPA), as a reference for a well-structured conceptual framework (Fig. 1d,
see Supplementary Fig. S2a, b for RIDMs derived from other brain regions).

We observed that the brain's RDM using voxels from HVC revealed two distinct clusters (Fig. 1d)
corresponding to living beings (red square) and non-living objects (purple square), reflecting a robust
semantic understanding of the concepts. When comparing the RDMs of DNNs (using the final output
representations), only the CLIP model exhibited partial alignment with the brain's RDM, showing a
discernible cluster for living beings (Fig. 1e). In contrast, the other models, while demonstrating strong
discrimination of concrete concepts (evidenced by superior classification capabilities), failed to capture
the broader semantic clusters of living and non-living entities. This suggests that without a meaningful
understanding of the relationships between concrete concepts, DNNs struggle to generalize to abstract
concepts, highlighting a critical limitation in their cognitive capabilities. We also found that using fMRI
signals from HVC to guide the model yielded significantly higher classification performance compared
to using voxels from the lower visual cortex (LVC) or the entire visual cortex (Supplementary Fig. S2c).
These results provide further evidence that the semantic structures in higher-level visual areas are critical
for model optimization.

Mental representation-guided supervision enables DNNs to learn human-like conceptual
representations

Previous analysis indicated that the inability to capture internal relationships between concepts might be
a key factor limiting DNNs' understanding of abstract concepts—a capability inherently embedded in
human cognition2. Instead of further scaling up model parameters, we proposed a mental representation-
guided supervision framework to transfer human conceptual structures to DNNs.

We hypothesized that the conceptual structure of objects could be represented with a graph, and both the
pretrained LMs and the human brain have formed their own conceptual structures based on learning. Then,
given a set of objects, we can align the LMs' conceptual graph to the human brain's with a graph
matching25 approach. Here we built an iterative optimization framework (Fig. 2a) to reshape the
conceptual structure of LMs through two main steps that are performed in an alternative manner: 1)
seeking the optimal correspondences between LMs and the human brain representations; 2) updating
representations to maximize structural similarity (Fig. 2b). To this end, our architecture consists of three
learnable modules, i.e., a fMRI encoder, an image encoder, and a graph neural network26. By differentiable
design, gradients can be backpropagated from the matching layers to the encoders during the training
procedure (see Methods for details).

While the number of concepts is large in the real world, we found that by aligning the conceptual graph
with a small set of objects, the alignment was well generated to unseen concepts. Here, using the CLIP
model as an example, we performed alignment between the brain and the CLIP model across 150 concrete
object categories, and evaluated the distances between the representations of the brain and DNN with 50
unseen classes (see Methods). As shown in Fig. 2c, as the mental representation-guided supervision
process evolves, the distance between brain and DNN representations decreased consistently for both the
concepts in the training concepts and unseen concepts in mostly linear processes (R2 = 0.86, Pearson's r
= –0.93 for training, and R2 = 0.83, Pearson's r = –0.91 for unseen), revealing good generalization to
unseen objects. The RDM of the 50 unseen classes also demonstrated similarity to brain's RDM
(Supplementary Fig. S3a), with a better conceptual structure of objects (Supplementary Fig. S3b, c). These
results suggested that mental representation-guided supervision learning approach effectively transferred
human's conceptual structures to DNNs.

Enhancement of abstract concept understanding

We next evaluated the model's ability to understand abstract concepts with and without mental
representation-guided supervision. As illustrated in Fig. 1a and b (Bottom), models trained with mental
representation-guided supervision demonstrated significant improvements in one-shot learning tasks for
abstract concepts (P < 0.0001, two-tailed paired t-test, n = 100 independent runs).

To further assess the understanding of abstract concepts at different levels of abstraction, we employed
the Silhouette Coefficient (SC)27 to measure the quality of representations on 50 unseen classes (n =
66,067 test samples). The SC score, ranging from −1 to 1, evaluates how well each sample fits within its
own cluster (intra-cluster distance) and how well it is separated from other clusters (nearest-cluster
distance). A higher SC indicates that objects within the same concept have similar representations, while
objects from different concepts are well-separated, reflecting a better understanding of conceptual
relationships. As shown in Fig. 3a, without mental representation-guided supervision, models exhibited
strong representation ability for concrete concepts (SC = 0.231 for the 50 leaf nodes) but showed a marked
decline in performance for middle-level (SC = 0.144 for the 8 middle-level nodes) and high-level concepts
(SC = 0.044 for the 3 high-level nodes). This suggests that while models excel at understanding concrete
concepts, they struggle with abstract ones.

In contrast, with mental representation-guided supervision, concept representation improved significantly
across all three abstraction levels (Fig. 3a, P < 0.0001, two-tailed paired t-test), particularly for abstract
concepts. The SC increased from 0.144 to 0.239 for middle-level concepts and from 0.044 to 0.127 for
high-level concepts. Notably, we observed a nearly linear correlation between the degree of structural
alignment (measured by Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) distance28, which quantifies the dissimilarity
between two metric spaces by comparing the pairwise relational structures; see Methods for
computational details) and the SC score (Fig. 3b). This strongly suggests that the enhanced conceptual
understanding stems from the alignment of the model's representational structure with the brain's
conceptual framework. Further improvements could be achieved by pushing the models' representational
structures to be more consistent with the brain. Together, these findings demonstrate that mental
representation-guided supervision effectively enhances models' capacity to conceptualize abstract
categories.

Emergence of human-like conceptual hierarchy

We further assessed the similarity between the conceptual hierarchy structures of humans and models
using the 50 unseen concepts. To this end, we utilized WordNet19, a comprehensive lexical database that
encodes conceptual-semantic relationships, as a representation of human conceptual hierarchy (Fig. 4a).
We compared this structure of the models with the 50 unseen concepts. Our analysis revealed that models
trained with mental representation-guided supervision exhibited concept similarity matrices (CSMs)
highly aligned with WordNet, whereas models without such supervision showed no such alignment (Fig.
4b; see Supplementary Tab. S1 for the row/column labels of CSMs). Note that each entry of the CSM
quantifies the similarity between a pair of concepts (see Supplementary for computational details). These
findings were consistent across different DNN architectures and brain signals from multiple subjects (Fig.
4b-d and Supplementary Fig. S4).

Additionally, we found that mental representation-guided supervision enabled models to exhibit human-
like judgments in concept similarity tasks. Specifically, we employed a triplet odd-one-out task, where
participants (human or DNN model) were presented with three images and asked to select the least related
one (Fig. 4e). Human judgment data were sourced from the THINGS database29, which contains 4.7
million triplet odd-one-out judgments across 1,854 objects from 12,340 participants. We compared the
similarity between human and model responses (see Supplementary for details). Results showed that
mental representation-guided supervision significantly improved the alignment between human
judgments and model behaviors (Fig. 4f), with accuracy increasing from 43.74% to 49.94% (P = 7.56 ×
10−97, two-tailed paired t-test).

Many current DNN models can be easily deceived by targeted pixel-level perturbations (adversarial
attacks), whereas humans are remarkably robust against such perturbations. The lack of robustness
highlights that DNNs fall short of human-like understanding concepts. Therefore, we used projected
gradient descent (PGD) attacks30 to evaluate the robustness of mental representation-guided supervised
models (Fig. 4g, see Supplementary for details). We observed that human-like conceptual hierarchy leads
to increased adversarial robustness for CLIP-base on abstract concepts, with adversarial accuracy
increasing from 50.82% to 68.95% (3 abstract concepts; P = 4.01 × 10−71, two-tailed paired t-test) and
10.98% to 14.79% (8 abstract concepts; P = 5.94 × 10−18, two-tailed paired t-test). Together, these results
demonstrate that mental representation-guided supervision enables models to develop human-like
conceptual hierarchy structures, significantly enhancing their ability to conceptualize abstract categories.

Human-like conceptual hierarchy enhances performance in complex cognitive tasks

We demonstrated that models endowed with human-like conceptual hierarchy structures achieve
significant performance improvements across a variety of complex cognitive tasks.

One-shot learning (OSL). We first evaluated the one-shot learning capabilities of the models at different
abstraction levels. As was mentioned, a central challenge in one-shot classification, is to rapidly
understand the concepts from only one example31. The problem can be more difficult when the concepts
become more abstract (Fig. 5a, see Supplementary). When there are only two abstract concepts of living
thing and non-living thing, CLIP-base with mental representation-guided supervision achieved an average
improvement of 20.5 ± 1.3% (mean ± s.d., averaged across S1-S3, P < 0.0001 for all subjects, two-tailed
paired t-test) in OSL performance, outperforming baseline models with 4.9 times more parameters (Fig.
5b). Mental representation-guided supervision achieved consistent performance gains across different
DNN architectures (CLIP10, SimCLR23 and DINOv29) and supervision using brain signals from different
subjects (Fig. 5b and Supplementary Fig. S5). Moreover, we found a nearly linear correlation between the
degree of structural alignment (measured by GW distance28) and the one-shot classification accuracy,
consistent across supervision using brain signals from different subjects (Supplementary Fig. S6).

Generalized out-of-distribution (OOD) recognition. Next, we examined how mental representation-
guided supervision enhanced the robustness of generalized OOD recognition (Fig. 5c, see Supplementary).
We defined a series of OOD recognition tasks (31 tasks, see Supplementary Tab. S2), which assess the
conceptual extrapolation ability of DNNs from minimal category supervision, such as determining
whether unseen categories (e.g., "bowling" and "carriage") should be classified as a broader category (e.g.,
"non-animal"). These tasks require models to capture high-level semantic structures that align with the
hierarchical structure of human conceptual knowledge. As shown in Fig. 5d, mental representation-guided
supervision significantly improved OOD robustness, yielding performance increases of 11.5 ± 4.7%, 13.6
± 9.3%, 9.1 ± 8.3% (mean ± s.d., averaged across 3 subjects and 31 tasks, P < 0.0001 for all subjects,
two-tailed paired t-test) for CLIP-base, SimCLR-base and DINOv2-base, respectively, without the need
for extensive supervision labels. Similar improvement trends can be found in different architectures across
varying parameter scales and supervision using brain signals from different subjects (Fig. 5d).

Brain-to-image and image-to-image retrieval. To intuitively assess the quality of the learned
representations, we evaluated the effectiveness of mental representation-guided supervision for both
brain-to-image (Fig. 5e, see Supplementary) and image-to-image (Fig. 5g, see Supplementary) retrieval
tasks. Brain-to-image retrieval, a common benchmark for neural decoding models24,32,33, evaluates the
ability to reconstruct perceived stimuli (n = 50 visual stimuli) from brain signals. Our approach
consistently improved decoding performance, achieving an average increase of 7.34%–26.67% in 50-way
retrieval across all subjects compared to existing decoding methods33–35 (Fig. 5f). Qualitative analysis of
brain-to-image retrieval on a subset of ImageNet-21K36 (n = 66,067 test samples, Supplementary Fig.
S7a-c) indicated the concept representations of DNNs can be predicted from fMRI patterns derived using
our mental representation-guided supervision framework. For example, the fMRI pattern evoked from an
image of "a man lying on a hammock" can be the image of "a child lying on the baby carriage" (the 5th
row, Supplementary Fig. S7a). In the case of "harp" (the 6th row, Supplementary Fig. S7a), although the
top retrievals fall into the wrong concrete categories, they are all related to "musical instruments". Similar
results can be found in most instances across different subjects (Supplementary Fig. S7b, c).

In image-to-image retrieval tasks (Fig. 5g, h), mental representation-guided supervision enabled models
to retrieve semantically similar objects despite significant visual differences, even when these objects
belonged to different predefined categories. For example, an image of a "beer mug" successfully retrieved
images sharing attributes like "cup" or "jug" from distinct categories (Fig. 5h, top row). Similar results
were observed across most instances, highlighting the model's enhanced ability to capture semantic
relationships beyond superficial visual features. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that human-like
conceptual hierarchy structures, facilitated by mental representation-guided supervision, significantly
enhance model performance in complex cognitive tasks.

Cognitive-level consistency of the learned conceptual manifold

To evaluate whether the latent embedding spaces, shaped by mental representation-guided supervision,
capture typical judgements for concepts, we generated a low-dimensional PCA-based space (conceptual
manifold; see Supplementary for details), and trained a GPT-2-based37 text decoder on the COCO
dataset38 (see Supplementary for details). This conceptual manifold allows us to assess cognitive-level
consistency for both seen and unseen points in the latent space, while the decoder reconstructs the
semantics of a given representation point as a sequence of words, enabling a detailed analysis of the
manifold's properties.

Local semantic consistency. We first assessed the local semantic consistency of the manifold, which
measures whether similar concepts are clustered together in the representation space. To this end, we
designed an out-of-distribution semantic coherence test (see Supplementary for details), evaluating the
semantic consistency and similarity between newly generated samples and their nearest real neighbors in
PCA space (Fig. 6a). This task can also be considered a zero-shot test of semantic coherence, since the
evaluations are performed in novel categories without explicit training. Note that in this study, zero-shot
(learning) means that performing a task on unseen samples, where the model is trained only on known
samples—not learning without any data. As shown in Fig. 6b, we found that the 2-D PCA points sampled
from different conceptual regions show strong semantic correlations with the real samples. For example,
we can reconstruct the semantics of T-shirt and tie within the "clothing" region and generate the semantics
of truck near the region associated with "vehicles". In contrast, models without brain supervision produced
semantically meaningless reconstructions (Supplementary Fig. S8a). By using 8 abstract categories as
ground-truth, we found that mental representation-guided supervision significantly enhanced local
semantic coherence, with semantic consistency accuracy improving by 15.9% and semantic similarity
scores increasing by 6.2% on average compared to the model without supervision (P < 0.0001, two-tailed
paired t-test, Fig. 6c).

Intersections between different concepts. We further investigated whether intersections between
different concepts yield meaningful reconstructions. By generating new points through interpolation
between two real samples from distinct concepts (Fig. 6d), we observed that the reconstructed semantics
aligned well with human intuition, exhibiting smooth and realistic transitions (Fig. 6e). For instance,
transitioning between "iPod" and "video recorder" resulted in a logical semantic shift from "television" to
"video recorder" (Fig. 6e, left), while interpolating between vehicles and ungulate animals produced the
concept of "horse" (Fig. 6e, right). Qualitative analysis indicates most of the key features of these concepts
can be effectively captured with a limited number of principal components, which is also reflected in the
reconstruction error and explained variance ratio (Supplementary Fig. S8b). These findings suggest that
mental representation-guided supervision ensures the conceptual manifold is semantically continuous and
smooth, enhancing the model's cognitive generalization capabilities.

Concept summarization and arithmetic. Finally, we evaluated the original latent space using two highly
challenging tasks: concept summarization (Fig. 6f) and concept arithmetic (Fig. 6h), which involves linear
operations on latent embeddings (see Supplementary for details). For concept summarization, the model
was tasked with generating a sentence to describe multiple input images. As shown in Fig. 6g, the
regulated manifold enabled the model to infer shared behavioral details and the number of objects. For
example, given a set of images depicting different types of animals lying on grass, the decoder with mental
representation-guided supervision was able to reconstruct the sentence of "animal laying on a grassy area".
Given a set of images, each depicting a close-up of a pair of different animals standing on grass, the
decoder successfully reconstructed the text "two animals standing in a grassy area".

For concept arithmetic (Fig. 6h), we tested whether mental representation-guided supervision could steer
generated captions toward desired conceptual directions through subtraction and addition operations. For
example, subtracting "motorcycle" and adding "horse" shifted the semantics from "a man riding a
motorcycle" to "a man riding a horse" (Fig. 6i, first case). Similarly, removing "dog" from "a dog playing
with a frisbee" and adding "a young girl" yielded "a young girl is playing with a frisbee" (Fig. 6i, second
case). In the third case, subtracting "banana" and adding "cell phone" transformed "a young girl holding
a banana" into "a young girl holding a cell phone."

These results demonstrate that mental representation-guided supervision produces a low-dimensional
conceptual manifold that aligns with human judgments, enabling accurate and intuitive descriptions of
objects along semantically meaningful dimensions. This advancement highlights the potential of brain-
guided approaches in creating models with enhanced cognitive generalization and interpretability.

---

## Methods

Datasets

fMRI data. BOLD signals are obtained from an open dataset DIR45, which are collected using a Siemens
MAGNETOM Verio scanner 3.0-Tesla from three healthy subjects. In image presentation experiments,
each subject viewed 1,250 unique images of natural scenes. These image stimuli are drawn from 200
representative object categories of the ImageNet dataset36, with 150 categories used for training and 50

Model architecture. Technically, like most representation learning practices, our first component
employs two nonlinear encoders (here, a ViT50 and a multilayer perceptron but can take any other form)
to map brain signals (fMRI) and image embeddings to new latent spaces (Fig. 2a). Next, a GNN34,51,52
with multi-head attention, which learns node representation for both fMRI and images (parameters are
shared across modalities; see Supplementary for details) is leveraged to predict an assignment matrix with
minimal Wasserstein distance47, resulting in initial correspondences between brain and model
representations. The representations in latent spaces are considered as graph nodes (entities). To reshape
embedding spaces of DNNs, we leverage a differentiable sampler (based on re-parametrization technique
Gumbel Softmax49) with the similarity scores between entities to construct local structures for each
putative correspondence. It is worth noting that the procedure of structure (edge) construction is
"dynamic" since node representations are evolving through the update of neural network parameters
during training. See Supplementary for the architecture configuration and hyperparameter settings.

By using relaxation techniques48,49, all calculation and optimization processes in the pipeline are
differentiable, enabling gradients to be backpropagated from the matching layers to the encoders. We
conduct mental representation-guided supervision on the DIR dataset. The stimuli (150 training categories
and 50 test categories) in DIR dataset are identical to those used in the GOD dataset24 but contain a larger
number of evoked fMRI recordings (6,000 training samples and 1,200 test samples). See Supplementary

Noteworthy results: (reviewers' summary)
Recent advances in deep neural networks (DNNs), especially large models (LMs) have skyrocketed their image and text
understanding as well as generation and classification performance. However, imitating the in depth interpretation and
abstract reasoning capacities of humans remains a major challenge.
This study challenges the ability of large neural network model architectures to capture and learn generalised concepts.
Since DNNs are usually trained to perform well on a clearly defined task, such as classification, they tend to lack the human-
like abstraction capacity. To this end, a brain-in-the-loop supervision framework was introduced, which aligns the DNN
embeddings with human brain activation structure. Specifically, fMRI brain signals were compared to the DNN image
embeddings via an encoder and graph neural network architecture. The improvement of generalization capabilities was
demonstrated in a series of tailored experiments providing evidence and supporting the claim that the semantic coherence of
DNNs can be enhanced by incorporating human conceptual structure into their training. Improved performance also involved
one-shot learning and out-of-distribution recognition.
Validity and Significance
This paper introduces a novel method of leveraging human brain-based representations to improve AI systems toward
human-level understanding. An iterative graph matching routine is introduced utilising Wasserstein distance and Gromov-
Wasserstein (GW) distance based loss functions (line 630 and 642 in the main text). The validity of the results is tested on
several state-of-the-art models including CLIP, SimCLR and DINOv2 showing that one-shot classification accuracy
improves significantly when brain-in-the-loop supervision is deployed, particularly for abstract concepts (see Fig.1 a-c). The
statistical robustness of the results is confirmed by two-tailed paired t-tests with adequate P-value scores.
Notably, the framework paves the way for integrating human-like abstraction capabilities into AI by means of its structural
alignment with biological neural activity.
Overall, the paper is very well written, with a lot of numerical results, providing a consistent picture about what has been
gained by including sparse brain-in-the-loop information into AI models.
Methodology and Data
In order to test the concept understanding of DNNs (without brain-in-the-loop) a one-shot learning experiment (Fig.1, a-c)
was conducted for concrete and abstract concepts and three different architectures with varying sizes. Increasing the model
parameter number yielded an improvement in the concrete concept classification, but only a negligible advantage in abstract
concept classification.
For the remaining set of experiments the networks were integrated into a composite architecture together with the fMRI
encoder of brain signals, training the encoders across 150 training categories and evaluating with 50 unseen ones. The
Silhouette Coefficients were computed to measure representation quality for concrete vs. abstract concepts demonstrating
enhanced conceptual alignment with brain-in-the-loop (Fig.3).
Furthermore, conceptual similarity matrices (CSM) of DNN’s representations with brain-in-the-loop demonstrate higher
similarity to WordNet’s conceptual hierarchy and odd-one-out accuracy rises by ~6% compared to the base model (Fig.4).
One shot classification and out-of-distribution recognition with brain-in-the-loop display higher accuracy for all considered
DNNs (Fig.5) and consistency tests on a PCA manifold also corroborate improved semantic robustness with brain-in-the-
loop supervision (Fig.6). Moreover, multiple tests, such as semantic summarisation, focusing on the conceptual manifold
confirmed its cognitive-level consistency and ordered organization of concepts. (also Fig. 6).
Altogether, the initial assumption that incorporating brain-in-the-loop optimization into large DNN image classifiers promotes
the model’s abstract conceptual understanding is more than well supported by the experimental evidence.
